problem: Existing VLN agents are trained on English-centric corpora and do not transfer to non-English or low-resource languages. A naive pivot approach (translate the instruction to English at test time) degrades sharply and depends on translation quality.
motivation: Users speak many languages, so instruction-following agents need to work beyond English. The authors observe that a pivot method trained on English only falls far below its English upper bound on RxR Hindi, which motivates a dedicated cross-lingual cross-modal VLN method.
key_idea: Build a machine-translation-augmented multilingual VLN dataset and train a shared cross-modal transformer (XLM-R instruction encoder) with cross-lingual and path-level contrastive losses so that different languages align through a shared vision and action context.
insight: Pivot (translate-then-navigate) baselines fall well short of the English upper bound, and their performance varies strongly with translation quality (M2M vs Helsinki). Aligning English and Hindi in a shared encoder gives consistent gains over the pivot baseline, larger with the better M2M translator. The authors admit the gain may partly come from extra training data rather than alignment, and no ablation separates the two.
method: MT-augmented data: translate English RxR instructions into other languages with machine translation to build a multilingual VLN dataset
Instruction encoder: XLM-R tokenization and embeddings for multilingual instructions
Visual/action encoders: 36-view panoramic ResNet features plus orientation; action look-up embeddings
Cross-modal transformer: fuses language, visual and action embeddings; an FC layer predicts the action
Domain-specific translator: multilingual BART trained interactively with the navigator to adapt translation to the navigation domain
Contrastive losses: language-level (same instruction in different languages as positives) and path-level (instructions of the same path as positives), temperature 0.1
Speaker-navigator co-training: a speaker reconstructs instructions from observation and action sequences; GPT-3 and BLIP are used for explanations (only described qualitatively)

setting.backbone: XLM-R instruction encoder + ResNet visual features + cross-modal transformer (CLIP-ViL based), trained
setting.training_data: RxR English instructions plus machine-translated (M2M / Helsinki-NLP) Hindi instructions

numbers.backbone: CLIP-ViL-based cross-modal transformer + XLM-R, Hindi translated with M2M
numbers.extra: Machine-translated multilingual training data; Hindi evaluation

numbers_note: Only preliminary Hindi results are reported, and the GPT-3/BLIP interaction component is qualitative only. The Val-Seen Helsinki VMLN row (SR 16.4, SPL 15.1, NE 13.26) is not listed separately.
results: On RxR Hindi val-unseen, VMLN with M2M translation reaches SR 24.4 / nDTW 41.0 versus the pivot baseline's 21.5 / 37.9. It stays far below the English upper bound of SR 36.3. With Helsinki translation, SR is 17.4 versus 15.0 for pivot.
limitations: Only preliminary results on Hindi; Telugu and zero-shot settings are untested, and the gain may come from extra data rather than alignment
The GPT-3/BLIP accessibility and explanation component is described but not quantitatively evaluated
Large gap to the English upper bound and strong dependence on translation quality; the method description is loosely written and inconsistent with the experiments
